questions.problem:
$$
x={R}^{-1}\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,b
$$

Let $A=QR$  be a QR decomposition of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$ with linearly independent columns, and the expression above gives the least-squares solution of $Ax=b.$ What is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the normal equation

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Then, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $R$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by ${R}^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{-1}\cdot Rx & ={R}^{-1}\cdot {Q}^{T}b \\ x & ={R}^{-1}\,\,{Q}^{T}\,\,b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing part of the equation is ${Q}^{T}.$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is orthogonal, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-11 \\ 2{x}_{2}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=5.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-4(5) & =-11 \\ 3{x}_{1} & =9 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & -1 \\ 2\sqrt{2} & -1 \\ \sqrt{2} & 4\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -4\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -4\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} & 2\sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 9 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2} & -4\sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}38\sqrt{2} \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-4\sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=38\sqrt{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-5.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1}-4\sqrt{2}(-5) & =38\sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{2}{x}_{1} & =18\sqrt{2} \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Given the QR decomposition $A=QR,$ find the least-squares solution to $Ax=b,$ where

$$
Q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & \sqrt{2} \\ 3\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{2} \\ 2\sqrt{5} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,R=\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Substituting $A=QR,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ (QR)^{T}QRx & =(QR)^{T}b \\ {R}^{T}({Q}^{T}Q)Rx & ={R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ has orthonormal columns, ${Q}^{T}Q=I,$ and we get

$$
{R}^{T}Rx={R}^{T}\,{Q}^{T}b.
$$

Finally, since ${R}^{T}$ is invertible, pre-multiplying by $({R}^{T})^{-1}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}Rx & =({R}^{T})^{-1}\cdot {R}^{T}{Q}^{T}b \\ Rx & ={Q}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{R}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}x & =\overset{{Q}^{T}}{\overset{⏞}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{70}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 3\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2} & 3\sqrt{2} & -5\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]}}\overset{b}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}} \\ [\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5} & 2\sqrt{5} \\ 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}-10\sqrt{5} \\ -10\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{2}{x}_{2}=-10\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-10.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}{x}_{1}+2\sqrt{5}(-10) & =-10\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5}{x}_{1} & =10\sqrt{5} \\ {x}_{1} & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the least-squares solution to $Ax=b$ is $[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -10\end{aligned}].$
